Built a shared deployed-tree fixture in run-all.sh (built once before any suite runs, lent read-only via chmod -R a-w, exported as RUN_ALL_SHARED_FIXTURE only when a declared consumer is selected) and common_test_fixture_overlay (lib/common.sh, cp -a --reflink=auto, never hardlinks) for a consumer that must mutate it. Investigated the realistic consumer set directly against each of the 38 core integration-classified suites' own content (not suite-classification.data's documented conservative textual-reference reason field) and found exactly one genuine consumer, test-deploy-orphans.sh, now migrated (8/8 assertions identical standalone and under the shared fixture). Added test-run-all-shared-fixture.sh (8 assertions) pinning build-once/never-built-when-unused/write-blocked; extended test-common-lib.sh with 6 assertions for common_test_fixture_overlay's own contract. Documented the shared-fixture contract in shell-script-testing.md, including the two-sibling-artifact (.claude-extensions.json, .syncprotect) overlay requirement discovered while migrating test-deploy-orphans.sh (an incomplete overlay misclassified the entire deployed tree as orphaned -- 743 false findings -- before the fix). Full redeploy + full verify-deploy.sh battery run twice, 39 checks / 0 failures both times, including gate 8's complete shell-suite battery. A mid-phase informal --jobs auto battery run surfaced 6 transient failures traced to a concurrent sibling process live-mutating specs/state.json/TODO.md during the run (host-state contention, logged, unrelated to this phase's own edits, not reproduced on either full deploy-headless.sh verification run). 7 of 20 plan phases remain [NOT STARTED] (Phase 14 next). Clean phase boundary, not a context-exhaustion handoff.

memory_candidates.content: Before chartering or executing a 'build it once, lend it read-only' shared-fixture consolidation for a test corpus, verify the realistic consumer count by reading each nominated suite's ACTUAL construction call (grep for a real, unflagged subprocess invocation against a scratch target), never by trusting a classification file's documented conservative/over-counting textual-reference scan. A suite that drives MULTIPLE or flag-varied real invocations of the heavyweight tool under test (fresh-vs-resync idempotency, a flag matrix, an equivalence proof) is categorically NOT a sharing candidate: the variance across its invocations IS what it verifies, and substituting a single shared artifact changes what the suite proves rather than merely how cheaply. In one real corpus this narrowed a textually-counted 38-suite 'integration' population down to exactly 1 genuine consumer.

When overlaying a cheap COPY of an already-deployed tree into a consuming test suite's own scratch target (instead of re-running the real deploy script), copy every top-level artifact the deploy process writes, not just its primary output subdirectory. A manifest/extension-driven deploy (e.g. deploy-headless.sh writing .claude/) commonly ALSO writes PROJECT-ROOT SIBLING files (here: .claude-extensions.json naming the active extension set, .syncprotect naming excluded paths) that downstream checks (here: find_orphans) read independently of the primary subdirectory. Omitting a sibling file makes those checks silently resolve an EMPTY declared/excluded set, misclassifying the entire copied tree (here: 743 false 'orphan' findings) -- a failure mode indistinguishable from a real defect until traced to the missing sibling artifact. Always diff a fresh real deploy's full top-level listing against what a 'cheap overlay' plans to copy before trusting the overlay is complete.

Implementing a 'fast copy of a read-only shared fixture that the copy's own consumer may then mutate' helper: use `cp -a --reflink=auto`, never `cp -l`/`cp -al` (hardlinks). A hardlink shares the SAME inode as the read-only source, so a subsequent `chmod` on the writable copy also changes the source's permission bits, silently defeating the read-only-lending contract the whole mechanism exists to enforce. `--reflink=auto` gives copy-on-write (independent inodes sharing data blocks) on a supporting filesystem and falls back to a plain deep copy elsewhere -- correct in both cases, unlike hardlinks which are a correctness hazard disguised as a performance optimization.
